newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch to publish tax reform plans for 21st century.
newsitem.headline: Dutch to publish tax reform plans for 21st century.

text.p: The Finance Ministry said on Friday the government would publish next month plans for major reforms of the Dutch tax system in the 21st century.
But it declined to comment on details of the plans reported by De Telegraaf newspaper.
A spokesman for Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm said the plans would be published in a 500-page document around September 16, when the 1998 budget is published.
He said they were aimed at broadening the range of sources for tax revenues, simplifying the system, reducing taxes on labour and keeping Dutch taxes competitive with taxes elsewhere.
As the plans are for the following century, they would be implemented by the government which takes office after elections scheduled for May 1998.
Zalm's spokesman declined to comment on a report in De Telegraaf that the plans would place further limits on the tax-deductibility of single-premium life insurance policies.

These are popular old-age savings vehicles in the Netherlands, attracting several billion guilders in premiums each year. This money has traditionally been invested in fixed income securities, but in recent years a growing proportion has been channelled into equities.
De Telegraaf said the top rate of personal income tax, currently 60 percent, could be cut to below 50 percent but that value added tax (TAX) on goods and services would be raised.
It said homeowners' mortgage interest payments would remain fully tax deductible.
Zalm's spokesman declined to comment on these points.
